source_refs.note: Topic 20.3.1 as printed, with Figure 20.6, the three For information boxes and the Applications of PCR (PDF 160-162).

blocks.text: First, an excessive amount of primer (a sequence of 20 to 30 nucleotides) is mixed with the DNA fragment (gene of interest). This mixture of primers and DNA is heated to about 98°C. At this temperature, the double-stranded DNA breaks into single strands. Each single stranded DNA can act as the template for the in vitro DNA synthesis.

The solution is allowed to cool to about 60°C. As it cools, the forward and the backward primers anneal or hybridize to the single-stranded DNA at its complementary regions. So, the rest of the fragment remains single-stranded.

A very heat-stable DNA polymerase, called Taq polymerase is added. All four types of nucleotides are also added. The Taq polymerase adds new nucleotides to the 3’ end of primer. In this way, it copies the rest of the fragment just like the replication of DNA. In this way, a complimentary copy of the entire single-stranded DNA has been added to the primer. Because both DNA strands are replicated, there are now two copies of the original DNA fragment.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints “complimentary copy”; the correct word is complementary (a copy whose bases pair with the template strand).

Steps 1 to 3 are repeated and the two copies become four. It is not necessary to add any more polymerase, as the heating does not harm this enzyme. Each cycle is completed in one or two minutes and it doubles the number of DNA molecules. After 20 cycles, a single fragment of DNA produces more than one million copies.

blocks.alt: A vertical flow. A double-stranded DNA with the gene of interest and free primers (P). Heat: 1- Denaturation separates the strands. Cool: 2- Annealing, a primer P binds to each strand. DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) and free nucleotides added: 3- Extension builds new strands, giving 2 copies (Cycle 1). Heat and cool again give 4 copies (Cycle 2), then 8 copies (Cycle 3). Old strands are blue, new strands red; the two original strands stay in two of the copies.
blocks.caption: Figure 20.6: Steps of PCR (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 20.6).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Gene of interest, Primers, Heat, Cool, 1- Denaturation, 2- Annealing, DNA polymerase (Taq polymerase) & Free nucleotides added, 3- Extension, 2 copies, 4 copies, 8 copies, Cycle 1, Cycle 2, Cycle 3.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 20.6 shows an original (parent) strand in three of the eight copies after cycle 3. There are only two parent strands, so only two of the eight copies carry one, as drawn above.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: PCR is also used to build genomic library. It is the collection of the total DNA from a single organism. Genomic libraries are commonly used for sequencing the DNA.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: The Taq polymerase is a temperature-tolerant enzyme isolated from Thermus aquaticus, a bacterium found in hot springs. This enzyme is stable and active at near-boiling temperatures.

blocks.title: For information
blocks.text: The optimum temperature for carrying out the extension of primer is 72°C. This step is completed in just one minute.

items: It is an efficient diagnostic technique used for detecting genotypes of infectious agents.
It is used to detect genetic mutations responsible for certain genetic diseases and cancers.
In criminal investigations, “DNA fingerprints” are prepared from the cells in a tiny sample of dried blood or at the base of a single human hair.
Physicians can detect genetic defects in very early embryos by collecting a few sloughed-off cells and amplifying their DNA.
PCR is also used to examine the DNA of extinct species, as long as even a minuscule amount of their DNA remains intact.
